newsitem.title: UK: NWE high sulphur fuel softer on swaps, pressured c.
newsitem.headline: NWE high sulphur fuel softer on swaps, pressured c.

text.p: European high sulphur fuel oil softened on Wednesday with barges closing lower on softer swaps and with some prompt cracked cargoes pressured by incoming Russian material, traders said.
High sulphur barges traded at $84 and $84.75 fob ARA for RMG material late in the day after earlier deals at $85.25 and $85, compared with Tuesday's range of $85/$86.
Some traders attributed the weakness to swaps coming off a little from Tuesday's levels, while others said barges were not looking too hot with two pressured cargoes on the market.
Others, yet, were more optimistic earlier in the day.

"We've been at this level, $85, for quite some time now and I think we may go higher a bit as there's basically good demand for bunkers and a few short positions to be covered and not too many cargoes around," one broker said.
"But again with so much manipulation in the market, who knows where things will head," he added.
Low sulphur barges were quiet but buyers and sellers moved closer together with some sellers slashing 50 cents off their asking price to $96.50 fob and buyers upping their bids some $1 to about $96.
High sulphur cracked cargoes were assessed steady, with offers in the $84/$85 region and bids a little lower, despite swaps falling a little early in the day.

A refiner was said to be holding an end month cracked cargo with a price tag of fob high plus $1, but two cargoes of lesser quality material with high water content were heard offered at $82 cif with the nearest bids in the $79/$80 range.
Traders said there was some pressure seen from some Russian material on the water.

"There's a little bit of pressure from one or two cargoes on the water which are pushing down the prompt cargoes a little bit but apart from that there's no major changes; swaps are down a little lower in NWE," the trader said.
One percent was steady although swaps came off a little. A U.K.-based refiner said he sold a large 70,000-tonne cargo a floating price to a trader who is taking it to the Mediterranean.
Traders said that in terms of fixed prices, low sulphur was assessed in the $92/$93.50 fob region after a deal on Tuesday for 50,000 tonnes of low sulphur at $92.50.
The buyer of that cargo was believed to be a U.K. major, who, according to shipping brokers, has fixed two vessels for taking two 50,000 tonne cargoes to the U.S. Gulf.
